summary:
ArpaSphere is a free, public web tool that lets anyone see how a patch of sky changes over time using NASA's SPHEREx data. Type a star name or coordinates, click the SPHEREx all-sky map, or open a link with coordinates in the URL. The tool fetches every SPHEREx image of that spot from NASA/IPAC IRSA, aligns them on the sky and plays them like a short video next to photographic plates from 1953 onward, so moving objects jump out. Click any object and the tool builds its 0.75–5 µm spectrum from up to 240 SPHEREx measurements, shows water and methane bands and estimates its type.

We tested it on all five challenge targets. Barnard's Star's 10.4″/yr track appears across 73 years. Epsilon Indi B's flux comes out at 27.1 mJy against 27.7 mJy expected. WISE 0855 appears only in the 4.4–5 µm detector. RW Aurigae and R Draconis saturate SPHEREx and are flagged as lower limits. On stars with known motion, 26 of 27 SPHEREx-only measurements agree with Gaia DR3 within 2σ. Because every SPHEREx release is queried live, new data appears without changing the code.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

- Pick a spot: search by name (156,000 stars and brown dwarfs built in, plus SIMBAD), enter RA/Dec, click the SPHEREx all-sky map, or open a URL such as https://sphere.arpama.tr/?ra=133.786&dec=-7.244&fov=5. Every view is shareable and embeddable.

- Watch it change: archive plates (POSS-I 1953, DSS2, 2MASS, WISE, Pan-STARRS) and SPHEREx frames grouped by observing period are resampled to the same north-up grid. Modes: blink, difference, stack and a swipe slider. Field of view 2′–60′, adjustable speed, export as GIF, PNG or video.

- Measure motion: the target is centroided in every SPHEREx frame and a weighted line is fitted to position versus time, with an uncertainty and a plot. Users can also click any star to measure it, or measure it themselves with two clicks on the oldest and newest frames.

- Automatic change scan: every star in the field is tracked; moving, appearing, vanishing and single-epoch sources are listed, moving ones are checked against Gaia DR3, and results export to CSV.

- Use the 102 bands: frames can be summed per detector (D1–D6) or shown as one band; false colour maps D1–2 to blue, D3–4 to green and D5–6 to red, so cold brown dwarfs look orange.

- Spectra on the fly: a Cloudflare Worker runs aperture photometry on small SPHEREx cutouts using each pixel's own wavelength (WCS-WAVE). The result is a 0.75–5 µm spectrum and a light curve with period search. Water (1.4/1.9 µm), methane (3.3 µm) and CO (4.6 µm) band depths are measured and a template fit estimates the spectral type.

- Overlays: Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 sources with proper-motion arrows, per-frame metadata and SPHEREx flag masks, Aladin Lite sky atlas, SkyBoT asteroid check.

- Other telescopes: CSA NEOSSat frames and CFHT/Gemini cutouts from the Canadian Astronomy Data Centre, aligned to the same scale.

- For everyone: easy mode with a glossary, expert mode, 1-minute tour, English/Turkish interface, light/dark themes, mobile layout.

HOW IT WORKS

A single HTML/JavaScript page with nothing to install. A Cloudflare Worker sits between the browser and the archives: it searches IRSA for every SPHEREx release, reads only the needed bytes of each ~70 MB file, runs photometry, resolves names through SIMBAD and caches results. FITS parsing, TAN-SIP astrometry, resampling, stacking and tracking run in the browser. The catalogue positions of 933 fast-moving stars were corrected against Gaia DR3 so the predicted tracks start in the right place.

VALIDATION

- Proper motion from SPHEREx alone: 26 of 27 reliable measurements agree with Gaia DR3 within 2σ (median difference 11%, direction 7°).

- Barnard's Star: 10.4 ± 0.8″/yr (catalogue 10.39″/yr).

- Epsilon Indi B: 27.1 mJy measured vs 27.7 mJy expected; water and methane detected; typed T1.5.

- Cepheid HV 1002: 30.5-day period recovered from SPHEREx alone (catalogue 30.48 d).

- Methane band depth tracks brown-dwarf type in 47 reliable T/Y dwarfs (Spearman ρ = 0.69).

- 100-field scan: 33,237 sources, 4,521 false movers rejected automatically; 42 candidates tested, none claimed as new.

HONEST LIMITS

SPHEREx pixels are 6.2″ and its baseline is about one year, so motion slower than about 2″/yr cannot be measured from SPHEREx alone. Stars brighter than about K = 9 saturate and are shown as lower limits. Automatically found sources are candidates until confirmed.

Overview page: https://explain.arpama.tr

Source code: https://github.com/Sertacerten06/Ataturk_soldiers

Tools and languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (no framework), Cloudflare Workers, Aladin Lite v3, Python for offline checks.
dataRefs: SPHEREx Level-2 images from every data release (NASA/JPL-Caltech/IPAC), accessed live through IRSA: per-pixel wavelength tables (WCS-WAVE), flags and variance are used for alignment, masking and on-the-fly spectra.
SPHEREx DR1 all-sky spectral cube and other IRSA HiPS surveys, used for the clickable all-sky map and the Aladin Lite sky atlas.
CatWISE2020 catalogue (NASA/IPAC IRSA): infrared positions and proper motions, drawn as motion arrows on the images and used by the discovery scan.
WISE / AllWISE / unWISE infrared imagery, shown as archive epochs between the 1953 plates and SPHEREx.
2MASS near-infrared imagery, used as an archive epoch.
NASA/IPAC IRSA services (SIA, IBE cutouts, TAP, HiPS) that the tool queries in real time, so every new SPHEREx release appears without code changes.
projectRefs: CSA (Canadian Space Agency) NEOSSat observations from the Canadian Astronomy Data Centre; daily frames are stacked, cleaned of the stripe pattern and shown side by side.
https://www.cadc-ccda.hia-iha.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/en/neossat/
Canadian Astronomy Data Centre (CADC): CFHT and Gemini image cutouts, aligned to the same scale with the target at its epoch position.
https://www.cadc-ccda.hia-iha.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/en/
ESA Gaia DR3: positions, parallaxes and proper motions used to check every motion we measure and to correct the catalogue positions of 933 fast-moving stars.
https://www.cosmos.esa.int/web/gaia/dr3
VizieR (CDS, Harvard mirror): Gaia DR3 catalogue access used for the catalogue-wide trajectory check.
https://vizier.cfa.harvard.edu/viz-bin/VizieR?-source=I/355/gaiadr3
Aladin Lite v3 (CDS Strasbourg): interactive sky atlas showing DSS2, 2MASS, AllWISE, SDSS and SPHEREx HiPS layers with our overlays.
https://aladin.cds.unistra.fr/AladinLite/
SIMBAD / Sesame (CDS, Harvard mirror): name resolution with position, proper motion, parallax and object type, and classification of discovery candidates.
https://simbad.harvard.edu/simbad/
STScI Digitized Sky Survey: POSS-I (1953) and POSS-II photographic plates, the oldest epochs in the time series.
https://archive.stsci.edu/cgi-bin/dss_form
Pan-STARRS1 imagery (STScI), used as an optical archive epoch around 2012.
https://panstarrs.stsci.edu/
Legacy Surveys viewer: unWISE infrared cutouts used as an archive epoch.
https://www.legacysurvey.org/
NASA SkyView: additional archive survey cutouts.
https://skyview.gsfc.nasa.gov/
IMCCE SkyBoT: known asteroids and comets in the field at each observation time, used to separate real minor bodies from artefacts.
https://ssp.imcce.fr/webservices/skybot/
HYG Database v4.2 (CC BY-SA 4.0): the built-in star catalogue for name search and target lists.
https://github.com/astronexus/HYG-Database
The UltracoolSheet v2.1.0 by Best, Dupuy, Liu et al. (CC BY 4.0): 3,798 M7–Y brown dwarfs and ultracool dwarfs in the catalogue.
https://sites.google.com/view/ultracoolsheet
Cloudflare Workers: the small server-side layer that proxies the archives, reads only the needed bytes and caches results.
https://workers.cloudflare.com/
